draft.title: Soaps and detergents
card: A soap molecule has two ends. The head is charged and hydrophilic (water-loving). The tail is a long hydrocarbon chain and is hydrophobic (water-hating) but oil-loving.
Grease and oil are non-polar, so they do not dissolve in water. The hydrocarbon tails of soap dissolve in the grease, while the charged heads stay in the water.
Many soap molecules surround a drop of grease with their tails pointing in and their heads pointing out. This forms a tiny ball called a micelle.
Micelles have a charged outer surface, so they repel each other and stay spread through the water. The grease is lifted off the surface and washed away.
draft.remember: Tails go into the grease, heads face the water, and the micelle carries the grease away.

a.q: Why does a soap molecule help water to remove grease from a plate?
opts: Its tail dissolves in grease and its head dissolves in water
Its head dissolves in grease and its tail dissolves in water
It reacts with the grease to make a new gas
It makes the grease polar so it dissolves in water
a.why: The non-polar tail mixes with the grease and the charged head mixes with water, so the grease is held in the water. The reverse arrangement is wrong because the charged head is hydrophilic and cannot enter non-polar grease.
a.clue: Match each end of the molecule to the substance it mixes with.

b.q: Soap is added to water containing a drop of oil. In the micelle that forms, which parts of the soap molecules face the water?
opts: The charged heads, on the outside of the micelle
The hydrocarbon tails, on the outside of the micelle
The charged heads, in the centre with the oil
The hydrocarbon tails, in the centre with the oil
b.why: The tails point inward into the oil, so the charged heads form the outer surface in contact with water. The last option is tempting because it names the tails in the centre, but it puts the heads in the oil, which is wrong.
b.clue: The oil sits in the centre, and the tails mix with it.

a.best: Its tail dissolves in grease and its head dissolves in water

b.best: The charged heads, on the outside of the micelle

problems.detail: Why (b) refers to 'the last option' even though options are shuffled. The distractor it describes (tails in the centre but heads in the oil) matches no option. The last option listed is 'The hydrocarbon tails, on the outside of the micelle', and the option naming tails in the centre is not a heads-in-oil arrangement. The explanation should name the wrong option by its content, for example 'The charged heads, in the centre with the oil'.
The clue 'The oil sits in the centre, and the tails mix with it' all but gives the answer away. It rules out every option except heads on the outside.
